sections.body: Course design and teaching is the part of artificial intelligence work that deals with how courses are planned, delivered, assessed and improved. In practice, AI systems now help draft learning outcomes, map topics to standards, generate quiz items and rubrics, summarise lecture notes into handouts, and power chatbots that answer course questions. These tools are used by instructors, instructional designers and teaching teams, often inside learning management systems or alongside them. The work is not mainly about replacing teachers, it is about reducing repetitive preparation and giving students more timely feedback. Current systems can produce plausible text and questions quickly, but they still need human review for accuracy, tone and fit with the curriculum. The field sits between education research, natural language processing and learning analytics.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this work are now routine, such as generating multiple choice questions from a passage, summarising notes into slides, and aligning a syllabus to a set of outcomes. What is not solved is the harder question of whether these outputs improve learning. Assessment generation can produce items that look valid but test recall rather than understanding, and automated scoring can inherit bias from training data. Personalised learning and early warning systems can flag students who may need support, yet they can also misread context and create stigma if used without care. Course-specific tutors can answer questions at any hour, but they may hallucinate facts, drift from the instructor's material, or fail to notice when a student is confused. The honest limits are evaluation, privacy, accessibility, and the difficulty of measuring cause and effect in real classrooms, and the site's library of 135 research papers links to original papers rather than a search tool when claims about teaching impact need checking.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes is the anchor page for anyone who needs to connect topics, standards and assessments into a coherent plan. Generating Assessments follows from that planning work and shows how AI can draft questions, rubrics and feedback prompts while keeping the instructor in control. Personalised Learning and Early Warning looks at adaptive pathways and risk signals, and it is the place to go for the ethical and practical questions that arise when systems try to predict student needs. Course-Specific AI Tutors covers the design of chatbots that are grounded in a particular syllabus, including how to constrain them and how to judge their answers. Lecture Materials from Notes deals with the production side, turning raw notes into slides, handouts and study guides. Together these pages move from course intent to assessment, then to personalisation, tutoring and materials, so a reader can start with the outcome they care about and follow the chain.
